lookForward.fits: The night Simchat Torah ends, Saturday 3 October 2026: second Hakafot in city squares and at the Western Wall, on the holiday weekend.
lookForward.headline: Saturday night: second Hakafot in the streets
lookForward.line: Simchat Torah ends Saturday evening; people go out to dance with Torah scrolls in city squares, live band included. At the Western Wall at 10pm, about a hundred scrolls, free of charge, or just stand and watch.

source.name: Western Wall Heritage Foundation: Sukkot in Jerusalem 2026

more: Hakafot are the circuits danced with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah. In the synagogue they happen twice, on the eve of the holiday and in the morning, without instruments, since the holiday itself forbids playing music.

The second Hakafot are what happens afterward. The moment the holiday ends, around seven this Saturday evening, playing music is allowed again, and the dancing moves outside: to a square, a lot, a closed-off street, with a band or orchestra, a microphone and speakers. It's a fairly young Israeli custom, a few decades old, and today almost every city holds one.

At the Western Wall, the second Hakafot begin at ten at night, with about a hundred Torah scrolls. In other cities it happens in the main square, usually from eight or nine, and the municipality posts the place and time on its website in the days before.

Entry is free everywhere, no need to register, and no need to know the words. Many people in the square don't dance at all, just stand to the side with a child on their shoulders, watching. Bring a water bottle, comfortable shoes, and head home early if you want. The next day, Sunday, everyone is back at work.

goodThing.fits: Chol HaMoed Sukkot: the whole country is on the road, and every year thousands get stuck along the way.
goodThing.headline: Stuck on the road? Help arrives in minutes
goodThing.line: Yedidim's volunteers unlock cars, change tires, or pull you from sand. Free, even at night. Call 1230.
more: Yedidim is a nationwide volunteer organization providing non-medical roadside help. Call 1230 from any phone, give your location, and the call center finds a nearby volunteer. Usually it's someone living ten minutes from you, with a kit in the trunk.

What they do: jump-start a dead battery, change a tire, open a car locked with the keys inside, sometimes with a baby inside, bring a little fuel or water, pull a car out of sand or mud, and help someone stuck in an elevator. What they don't do: medical treatment. For that, call 101.
The organization has more than 65,000 volunteers, and the service is free. No bill at the end, no subscription to buy in advance.

During Chol HaMoed this is especially useful. Families are on the road, the car is packed, the seats are full of sand and dust, and one kid presses the wrong button. Worth saving the number in your phone now, before you need it, and saying it out loud to the kids in the back seat.

onThisDay.fits: 1 October 1947: Aaron Ciechanover, the Nobel laureate in chemistry, was born in Haifa, and next week this year's Nobel Prizes are announced.
onThisDay.headline: Born: the researcher who found how cells clear waste
onThisDay.line: Aaron Ciechanover, in Haifa. At the Technion, with Avram Hershko, he found how cells tag unwanted protein for breakdown. Nobel Prize, 2004.

funFact.fits: Sukkot is the harvest festival, and the date harvest in the Arava and the Jordan Valley finishes exactly these weeks.
funFact.statement: More than half the world's Medjool dates grow in Israel.
funFact.reveal: By the Ministry of Agriculture's survey, about 28,000 tons of the world's roughly 45,000, mostly from the Arava and the Jordan Valley.

calmRead.fits: Expands today's On this day: Aaron Ciechanover, born today in 1947, and his discovery at the Technion.
calmRead.title: The one who cleans up the cell
calmRead.teaser: Two researchers in Haifa asked how the cell discards unwanted protein, and won a Nobel.
paragraphs: Aaron Ciechanover was born in Haifa seventy-nine years ago today, to parents who had immigrated from Poland. He studied medicine in Jerusalem, then went back north, to the Technion, for a doctorate under a young researcher named Avram Hershko.

In the 1970s, nearly the whole world was studying how the cell builds proteins. Hershko and Ciechanover asked the opposite question, the one almost nobody cared about: how the cell gets rid of a protein that has already finished its job. The answer was surprising. Breakdown doesn't just happen quietly in the background; it takes energy, exactly like building does.

What they found, together with Irwin Rose of Philadelphia, was a tagging system. A small protein called ubiquitin attaches to the spent protein, like a note, sometimes a whole chain of notes. A large machine inside the cell, the proteasome, reads the note and breaks down what's been marked into pieces that can be reused. Not a pile building up in a corner, but an organized collection system.

Without this system, cells couldn't divide, the immune system wouldn't recognize viruses, and damaged proteins would pile up. The discovery also led to new drugs, including one for a severe blood disease that deliberately blocks that same machine.
In 2004 the two shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Rose, becoming the first Israelis to win a Nobel Prize in science. Next week, Stockholm begins announcing this year's winners.

And these days, at the end of a holiday whose last act is taking the sukkah apart and putting the boards back in storage, there's something comforting in that: breaking down is also work, and it also takes strength.

word.fits: Sukkot, called the harvest festival in the Torah, and the last day of Chol HaMoed.
word.meaning: Gathering the harvest from the field at summer's end. The Torah calls Sukkot the festival of the asif, marking the end of one farming year and the start of the next.

kindness.fits: Chol HaMoed, with everyone on the road.
kindness.text: If you see someone standing by the roadside with the hood up, stop and ask if they need anything, even if you don't know anything about cars.

joke.setup: Why do they play instruments at the second Hakafot but not the first?
joke.punchline: Because on the holiday itself, only feet are allowed. The speakers wait outside.

riddle.fits: The date harvest in the Arava, finishing these very weeks.
riddle.riddle: I grow where it's hottest, picked from a ladder, and most of the world's supply grows right here. What am I?
riddle.hint: In the Arava and the Jordan Valley.
